The Savoy Male and Female College      61

solid white on the outside with the inside walls of a soft cream trimmed in a deeper cream.

    The classrooms were equipped with double desks, not screwed to the floor. At one end of each room was a large rostrum, below which were very long benches called "the recitation benches." Across the back of each rostrum extended a long blackboard. There were also coat-hooks for the students hung their hats and "cloaks" on hooks screwed over the walls.

    In addition to the buildings used for instruction, the institution owned a number of other outbuildings, and Benjamin County's buggy black land making good walks as an absolute necessity.

    In addition to the buildings used for instruction, the institution owned a number of outbuildings. These were of log construction, which were provided as bachelor's halls for young men who did not wish to room in town, living in them and doing their own housekeeping and cooking. These "back halls" as students called them, were considered the college campus on the east.

The Library.—The College library, according to a catalog probably representing the school near its zenith, consisted of "several hundred volumes." The Savoy College was listed in The Plainsman Messenger as "to become one of the public documents by Congress," this being a beneficial addition to the library of a college that was destined to become public men. The following story from The Plainsman Messenger suggests that the library was a matter of school pride and that efforts to increase it were a matter of administrative concern:

    Our library received twenty-six books last week.
notes: Page 61 of printed book. Describes classroom furnishings and college outbuildings, then introduces the college library. References The Plainsman Messenger. 'Benjamin County' may be a misread — likely Grayson County. The library reportedly had 'several hundred volumes.'
